name: Gusle
material: Maple bowl, single horse-hair string, horse-hair bow
powers: Accompanied heroic epic song in the oral tradition of the southern Balkans.
description: The gusle is a single-stringed bowed instrument of the southern Balkans, a round or pear-shaped bowl of maple or other wood covered with a skin, with a single horse-hair string played with a horse-hair bow, used to accompany the chanted epic poetry of the South Slavs. The singer, the guslar, plucks or bows the one string as he recites long heroic songs of battles, outlaws, and ancestral heroes, and among Croats, Serbs, Bosnians, and Montenegrins the instrument is inseparable from the living tradition of oral epic that Milman Parry and Albert Lord made famous with their studies of formulaic composition in the 1930s. In the Croatian lands the gusle was long carried by singers of the Dinaric highlands and the coast, and it has served both as a patriotic symbol and, at times, as an instrument of political song. The one-stringed fiddle is among the simplest instruments of European folk music, yet it carries an oral tradition of exceptional depth.
source: Ethnographic documentation of the South Slavic epic tradition

name: Croatian Nosnja
material: Linen, wool, and embroidery, varying by region
powers: Carried the wearer's village, age, and marital status in its cut, colour, and embroidery.
description: The nosnja, the traditional folk costume of the Croatian regions, is worn on feast days, at weddings, and at folklore festivals, and each district had its own cut, fabric, embroidery, and colour code that told the wearer's village, age, marital state, and even family at a glance. The dress is built from linen, hemp, and wool, spun, woven, and embroidered at home, and on it appear the characteristic Croatian embroideries, from the gold-worked caps of Posavina to the red-and-black geometric designs of the Dalmatian hinterland and the ornate festive dress of Slavonia. The nosnja belongs to the wider Balkan tradition of festive clothing, but its regional variety made it, in the 19th century, a badge of national identity during the Croatian national revival. It is still made by hand and worn with pride, and the rich costumes of the folk ensembles are among the most recognisable images of Croatian folklore. It is a garment of identity rather than a single mythic object.
source: Ethnographic documentation of Croatian regional costume

name: Mărțișor
description: Mărțișorul is the Romanian March talisman, a red-and-white twisted silk thread finished with a small charm, coin or bead, given on 1 March as a wish of health, love and good luck for the coming year. The name and the month both come from martie, March, and folk memory links the custom to the return of spring and to the capricious weather-woman Baba Dochia, whose shepherding stories echo the alternating mild and cold spells of early spring. Worn on the wrist or pinned to the chest for the whole month, the mărțișor is taken off at the end of March and tied to the branch of a fruit tree, believed to bring the tree good luck and fertility. The tradition is shared with the neighbouring lands that joined the joint UNESCO file of 2017, and Romanian jewellers now cast the charms in gold and silver alongside the older coins and shells.
material: red and white silk thread, metal charm or coin
source: Romanian ethnography of spring customs and UNESCO files

name: Troiță
description: Troița is the wayside cross of Romania, a hand-carved wooden cross sheltered under a little roof, erected at crossroads, springs, bridges and village edges to protect travellers and to honour the dead. In the wood-carving country of Maramureș the crosses are true monuments, their beams covered with vine scrolls, geometric rosettes, suns and sometimes the image of the Crucified, with inscriptions naming the dead and the year, and the oldest surviving examples go back to the eighteenth century. The cross is set up by families for a departed relative, at the place of a sudden death, or as a vow, and passers-by cross themselves before it, so the troița stands at the meeting of Christian devotion and the old belief that crossroads and water were liminal, dangerous places. New troițe are still carved and raised every year, making the wayside cross a living school of Romanian folk woodcarving.
source: Romanian ethnography of folk architecture and religion

name: Dacian Gold Bracelets
description: The Dacian gold bracelets are heavy spiral arm rings of the ancient kingdom of Dacia, hammered from Transylvanian alluvial gold in the mid-first century BC and worn as ornaments and marks of rank, possibly also deposited as votive offerings. The surviving pieces, each forged from a single ingot into five to seven coils that end in serpent or animal heads, weigh between roughly 680 grams and nearly 1.2 kilograms, a concentration of royal wealth unmatched in the Balkans. Around two dozen were looted from ritual pits near the sacred precinct of Sarmizegetusa Regia, the Dacian capital in the Orăștie Mountains, between 1999 and 2001 and smuggled abroad; an international police operation has since recovered at least thirteen, and others remain missing. The recovered bracelets are displayed in the Historical Treasury of the National History Museum of Romania in Bucharest as masterpieces of Dacian goldwork.
source: Archaeological studies of the Sarmizegetusa Regia treasure
